issues.title: Semi-discrete uniqueness lacks a twist hypothesis

failure_location.quote: Then the Monge problem \eqref{eq:Monge} has a unique solution $T$ given by

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $c$ be a cost function such that for all particle $i$, $c_i : y\in \Omega \mapsto c(y,\bm{x}_i)\in [0,+\infty) $ belongs to $C^{1,1}(\Omega)$.

issues.failure_explanation: Take two distinct target points with positive masses and let c≡0. Each c_i satisfies the stated C^{1,1} hypothesis, but every admissible partition map has cost zero, so the Monge solution is not unique. Moreover, no choice of Laguerre weights can simultaneously give both cells positive prescribed volume and null intersection. Thus the cited uniqueness result is being used without a necessary tie-excluding hypothesis.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem does not justify a unique partition for the full advertised class of C^{1,1} costs, and its theorem-based support for the preferred-shape corollary likewise requires a nondegeneracy condition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a standard tie-exclusion hypothesis to thm:semidiscrete: for every i ≠ j and every real a, the set {y : c(y,x_i) − c(y,x_j) = a} must have Lebesgue measure zero. Include the zero-cost medium among the compared costs when deriving lemma:prefferedshape. The stated uniqueness, null-intersection, and preferred-shape conclusions may then be retained in the regular regime.
issues.why_classification: C^{1,1} regularity alone does not exclude positive-measure ties, but tie-nullity is a short, standard nondegeneracy qualification. It excludes precisely exceptional cases in which uniqueness is impossible and leaves the method and affected regular-case conclusions unchanged. A missing mathematical premise must be supplied, so this is not a typo.

issues.title: Power-cost figure invokes the theorem outside its regularity regime

failure_location.quote: As a first static example, Fig.~\ref{fig:tessellations} shows three examples of a tessellation of a square periodic domain obtained by Theorem~\ref{thm:semidiscrete} with different cost functions and different particles shapes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: a power cost $c(\bm{x},\bm{x}_i) = |\bm{x}-\bm{x}_i|^{\alpha_i}$ where the $\alpha_i$ are distributed uniformly between 0.5 and 4.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the figure is obtained by thm:semidiscrete. That theorem, as stated, supports only costs c_i∈C^{1,1}(Ω). The figure's parameter range includes α=0.5 and other α<2, for which |x−x_i|^α is not C^{1,1} at x_i; for α≤1 it is not even differentiable there. In addition, the old periodic convention uses a minimum-distance function that is nondifferentiable at its cut locus. Thus the cited theorem does not support the stated experiment, although the separate discrete numerical construction can still produce an allocation.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical tessellation may remain a valid computed output, but its existence and properties are not justified by the theorem cited in the old prose.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the assertion that the periodic power-cost panel is obtained from thm:semidiscrete with the source-supported statement that it was computed by the fully discrete allocation procedure. Limit the claim to that numerical output and do not infer continuous existence or uniqueness from thm:semidiscrete for these nonsmooth costs.
issues.why_classification: The exponents below 2 and the periodic cut locus are substantial parts of the advertised example, not isolated degeneracies. This repair preserves the figure without new proof architecture, but it relinquishes the theorem-backed continuous guarantee. That is a limited substantive weakening of a recognizably comparable claim, making the issue moderate rather than minor or serious.

issues.title: Preferred-shape proof assumes an unjustified unique threshold

failure_location.quote: since the function $U : w \mapsto |\mathscr{S}(w)|$ is non-decreasing, $U(0)=0$ and $U(w)\to1$ as $w\to+\infty$ there exists a unique $w^*>0$ such that $U(w^*) = v_i$.

issues.failure_explanation: For the admissible constant cost c≡1 and any target volume v_i strictly between zero and one, U(w)=|{c≤w}| equals zero for w<1 and one for w≥1. Hence no w satisfies U(w)=v_i, even though every shape of volume v_i has the same energy. The proof's inference from non-decreasing behavior and endpoint limits to a unique threshold is therefore invalid, and the lemma's exact-sublevel conclusion fails for costs with positive-measure plateaus.
issues.overall_effect: The old source does not establish that every fixed-volume minimizer is an exact sublevel set with a unique threshold. The conclusion remains valid for suitably nondegenerate costs such as the intended smooth examples.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State lemma:prefferedshape under the standard no-plateau condition that every level set {x : c(x,x_i) = t} has Lebesgue measure zero. Replace the invalid monotonicity inference by the resulting continuity and strict increase of U on the attained range; the existing exchange argument then yields the unique exact sublevel minimizer.
issues.why_classification: The defect requires a genuine hypothesis and proof check, but excluding positive-measure plateaus is a local nondegeneracy qualification that preserves the fixed-volume minimization statement for the intended smooth costs. No new construction or downstream proof architecture is needed, so the complete repair is minor.

issues.title: Transport-gradient formula reverses the cost arguments

failure_location.quote:
On the practical side, it has been shown in \cite{xin_centroidal_2016} that the gradient of the total transport cost has a simple computable expression, namely
\[\nabla_{\bm{x}_i} \mathcal{T}_c(\hat{\mu}) = \int_{\mathscr{L}_i} \nabla_{\bm{x}_i} c(\bm{x}_i,\bm{x})\dd \bm{x}.\]

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that ∇_{x_i}T_c equals the integral of ∇_{x_i}c(x_i,x). The old energy actually establishes an integrand c(x,x_i), so differentiating with respect to x_i acts on the second argument and gives ∇_{x_i}c(x,x_i). These expressions coincide for the symmetric isotropic costs used in nearby examples but differ for the arbitrary asymmetric costs the framework permits.
issues.overall_effect: The abstract gradient-descent equation remains correct, but the supplied executable force is wrong for asymmetric costs; the symmetric numerical examples are unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the displayed transport-gradient formula, replace the integrand ∇_{x_i}c(x_i,x) by the derivative of c(x,x_i) with respect to its second argument, equivalently ∇_{x_i}c(x,x_i).
issues.why_classification: The old energy and Monge convention consistently use c(x,x_i), so the corrected argument order is uniquely forced directly by the source. No inference or construction changes, and the following isotropic formula already agrees with this reading. The error is therefore transcriptional.

issues.title: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics violates nonnegative amplitudes

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the elongation range (amplitude) of the protrusion $\xi_k$ is constrained by $\xi_k\geq0$

issues.failure_explanation: For nonnegative initial data, the solution of dξ=−ξdt+dB has a Gaussian noise term with positive variance and therefore has positive probability of becoming negative; from ξ_0=0 that probability is one half at every positive time. Thus the executable stochastic rule fails its required invariant ξ_k≥0.
issues.overall_effect: The random-protrusion simulation can produce coefficients that are negative and hence no longer represent the stated nonnegative protrusion amplitudes.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace each amplitude equation by a reflected Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, dξ_k = −ξ_k dt + dB_t^k + dL_t^k with ξ_k ≥ 0, where L_t^k is nondecreasing and increases only when ξ_k = 0, and use a reflection-consistent time discretization. This retains random creation and mean retraction while enforcing the stated amplitude invariant.
issues.why_classification: Nonnegativity fails with substantial probability, so this is not an exceptional-case qualification. Reflection gives a contained complete repair with no major loss, but it introduces a genuinely different stochastic process, a boundary regulator, and a corresponding numerical rule; that nontrivial local construction makes the issue moderate.

issues.title: Undefined junction point in the triple-junction force

diagnostic_evidence.quote: a force acting on each triple junction point $\bm{z}_{ijk}$ between three distinct particles $i,j,k$

issues.failure_explanation: The construction introduces the triple-junction point as z_{ijk}, and the force is indexed by z_{ijk}, but every direction vector on the right-hand side uses an unindexed z that is never defined. Consequently, the executable force formula has an undefined input. The immediate context uniquely identifies the intended point as z_{ijk}.
issues.overall_effect: The old triple-junction force is not literally executable as written, although its intended junction-point correction is evident and no formal result depends on it.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace every unindexed z on the right-hand side of eq:triplejunctionforce by the indexed junction point z_{ijk}.
issues.why_classification: The immediately preceding sentence and the force's own index uniquely identify z_{ijk} as the intended point. The replacement only repairs an undefined symbol and requires no change to the force construction or any mathematical inference, so it is a typo.

issues.title: Mean-field transport formula uses an unjustified gradient inverse

failure_location.quote:
it is well-known that the Monge problem $T\# f = \mathrm{Leb}$ has a unique solution which is of the form 
\[T(\bm{x}) = \bm{x} - (\nabla\ell)^{-1}(\nabla\Phi(\bm{x})),\]

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We also assume that the cost is of the form $c(\bm{x},\bm{y}) = \ell(\bm{y}-\bm{x})$ for a convex function $\ell$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the Monge problem has a unique map represented using (∇ℓ)^{-1}, while the old paper assumes only that ℓ is convex. What the old assumptions actually establish is insufficient: for ℓ≡0, the gradient is constant, the inverse is undefined as a function, and the zero transport cost cannot select a unique map. The formula therefore requires an injectivity condition such as differentiable strict convexity, which is a material restriction on the cost class.
issues.overall_effect: The transport-map representation and the ensuing Fokker–Planck–Monge–Ampère derivation are not well-defined for all convex costs claimed by the old text.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the mean-field cost assumption to a differentiable, strictly convex Legendre-type function ℓ for which ∇ℓ is injective and its inverse is defined on the relevant range; impose the additional C² regularity used in the Hessian and Monge–Ampère formulas. Carry these assumptions through the transport-map representation and the ensuing PDE derivation.
issues.why_classification: These assumptions make the inverse-gradient representation and subsequent derivation well-defined without changing the proof architecture. However, passing from arbitrary convex costs to an injective-gradient Legendre class excludes natural, substantial convex costs with flat directions or nondifferentiability. The same PDE chain survives for a broad comparable class, so the loss is limited but substantive and the issue is moderate.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: We also assume that the cost is of the form $c({x},{y}) = \ell({x}-{y})$ for a strictly convex function $\ell:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,+\infty)$.
